# picocom

**The minimal terminal-native serial console**

- **Version recorded:** 3.1
- **Categories:** `serial-terminals`, `workstation`
- **Upstream:** <https://github.com/npat-efault/picocom>

## What it does

picocom: a tiny, keyboard-only serial terminal that runs in your shell -- open a device at a baud rate and talk to it.

## Why you would want it

The unixy answer: no GUI, nothing to configure, ideal over SSH into a headless station or on a Pi. What experienced operators reach for once the GUI novelty wears off.

## Before it will work

Access to the serial device -- membership of the `dialout` group, which the workstation profile arranges. A programming cable or rig data port.

## Install and launch

- **Installed by name only** — it is in no profile.
- **Install:** `hammunition install picocom --dry-run`, read the plan, then run it without `--dry-run`.
- **Launch:** Its package ships its own commands and application-menu entry; a unit that ships none gets a generated terminal entry (**D-050**). `hammunition status` lists what is installed.
- **The install needs the network to:** your distribution's package archive.

## Offline use

*Not yet documented for this application.* Read “Before it will work” above for what it needs; the install-time network line above is the only offline fact generated from the manifest. Internet, a local network and a radio link are three different things, and this page does not claim any of them works until it says so.

## How it installs

- apt: `picocom`

## Known problems

Escape sequences (Ctrl-A Ctrl-X to quit) take a moment to learn; the manpage is short and complete. Needs `dialout`.

## Keeping it current

- probe: apt policy
- strategy: apt_upgrade

The picocom project on GitHub.
